entry: Government policy dividing a jurisdiction into zones, each with its own rules for permitted land use and development. Zones may be limited to one use, such as residential or industrial, may combine compatible activities, or, in form-based zoning, may regulate the density, size and shape of buildings. Most zoning systems allow variances, or exceptions, where a perceived hardship arises from the nature of a property. Zoning is the most common regulatory method of [[Urban planning|urban planning]] used by local governments in developed countries, though the United Kingdom and the city of [[Houston]], Texas, are exceptions. Ancient walled cities separated activities by type, and the [[Age of Enlightenment]] and [[Industrial Revolution]] greatly increased urban regulation. The planned city of [[Adelaide]], South Australia, used a park to separate its center from its suburbs. Supporters argue that zoning keeps nuisances such as factories away from homes and protects property values, while critics contend that density limits and minimum lot sizes restrict housing supply and raise prices.

Facility where animals are kept in [[Enclosure|enclosures]] for exhibition, and often for breeding and conservation. Short for zoological garden, the term zoo was first used of the London Zoological Gardens, which opened for scientific study in 1828 and to the public in 1847. Zoos vary greatly in size, from small urban enclosures of a few acres to open-range reserves spanning thousands of acres. The first modern zoo was the Tierpark Hagenbeck, created by Carl Hagenbeck in [[Germany]]. Ancient rulers kept menageries, and by the 4th century BC zoos existed in most Greek city states. In the [[United States]] alone, zoos are visited by over 181 million people annually. Animal welfare organizations have criticized housing conditions and the effects of visitor behavior, and efforts to improve conditions have been made in recent decades.

[[Paraphilia]] marked by a sexual fixation on non-human animals. The term is often used interchangeably with bestiality, but bestiality describes sexual acts with animals whether or not the person is attracted to them. Some studies have found that a preference for animals is rare among people who engage in sexual contact with animals. Krafft-Ebing introduced the term in *Psychopathia Sexualis* (1886). It was estimated to occur in 2% of the population in 2021.

Iranian religious reformer and prophet, the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism, also called Zarathushtra or Zarathustra. He challenged the tenets of ancient Iranian religion, and he is traditionally credited with the Gathas, the oldest Zoroastrian scriptures, in which he appears as a preacher and poet-prophet. According to Zoroastrian tradition, he trained as a [[Priest|priest]] and, around age 30, received a revelation of Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, and of the dualism of truth (asha) and deception (druj). He is said to have gained royal patronage under King Vishtaspa. Little is known of his life, and scholars disagree on when he lived. Zoroastrian texts portray his philosophy as emphasizing [[Free will|free will]], ethical responsibility and alignment with asha. Some have claimed, with much scholarly controversy, to find his influence in [[Plato]], [[Pythagoras]] and [[Heraclitus]], and in the [[Abrahamic religions]].

Hungarian-American socialite and actress. Born Sári Gábor in [[Budapest]], she emigrated to the United States in 1941 and became a sought-after actress with "European flair and style." Her first film role was in *Lovely to Look At* (1952), and the same year she appeared in *Moulin Rouge*, her most famous film. She was celebrated for her glamour and nine marriages, including to hotel magnate Conrad Hilton and actor George Sanders. During a layover in [[Omaha, Nebraska|Omaha]], she told the [[Associated Press]] that she had danced with [[Adolf Hitler]] twice.

Summer squash, *Cucurbita pepo* var. *cylindrica*, harvested while its seeds and rind are still immature and soft. Mature fruit can reach nearly 1 meter (3 feet), but zucchini are normally harvested at 15–25 cm (6–10 in). Botanically the fruit is a pepo, a [[Berry (botany)|berry]] with a hardened rind; in cookery it is treated as a vegetable. Zucchini descend from squashes first domesticated in [[Mesoamerica]] more than 7,000 years ago, but the zucchini variety was cultivated in northern Italy in the second half of the 19th century and was first described under that name in a work published in [[Milan]] in 1901. Italian immigrants almost certainly brought it to the United States, where the first records date to the early 1920s. Called courgette in France and Britain, it is usually cooked, but overmature or stressed plants can contain toxic cucurbitacins that make them extremely bitter and cause severe gastrointestinal upset.

Nguni ethnic group of southern Africa, the largest ethnic group in [[South Africa]], living mainly in [[KwaZulu-Natal]]. The Zulu began as a minor clan founded around 1574 among Nguni communities that took part in the Bantu migrations. In 1816 the Zulu formed a powerful state under [[Shaka]], who built a militarized system with conscription, a standing army and regiments organized by age. Zulu expansion was a major factor in the Mfecane upheavals across [[Southern Africa]]. Ceremonies such as the Umhlanga, or Reed Dance, and beadwork that signals identity remain central to Zulu culture. Today the Zulu are predominantly Christian, and many have created a syncretic religion that combines Christianity with their earlier beliefs.

Largest city in [[Switzerland]] and capital of the canton of Zurich, at the northwestern tip of Lake Zurich (pop., 2025: 440,935). Evidence of early settlement in the area dates back more than 6,400 years. Permanently settled for over 2,000 years, it was founded by the Romans as Turicum. During the [[Middle Ages]] it gained the status of imperial immediacy, and in 1519 it became a primary center of the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]] in Europe under [[Huldrych Zwingli]]. Zurich is a hub for railways, roads and air traffic, and its airport and main railway station are the largest and busiest in the country. Operations of 7 of the 10 globally leading AI companies, together with [[ETH Zurich]], make it a significant center for technology development. It also leads continental Europe as a financial and insurance center. Its museums include the Swiss National Museum and the Kunsthaus.

Former division or [[Phylum|phylum]] of the kingdom Fungi, now split between the phyla Mucoromycota and Zoopagomycota. The name refers to the zygosporangia formed in sexual reproduction, in which resistant spherical [[Spore|spores]] form after two [[Hypha|hyphal]] strands fuse. Most members are terrestrial, living in soil or on decaying plant or animal matter. Some are parasites of plants, insects and small animals, while others form symbiotic relationships with plants. Zygophores, the sex organs, grow toward each other under the guidance of volatile [[Pheromone|pheromones]] until their walls adhere. Asexual sporangiospores are dispersed when thin sporangium walls are broken by raindrops or passing animals. The group is no longer recognized because it is not believed to be truly monophyletic.

Irish statesman, born in New York City, who served three terms as [[Head of government|head of government]] and as president of Ireland from 1959 to 1973. He was a commandant of the Irish Volunteers at Boland's Mill during the [[Easter Rising]] of 1916 and was sentenced to death, but he was released, partly because of his American citizenship. After leading Anti-Treaty Sinn Féin until 1926, he founded Fianna Fáil, which abandoned abstention from *Dáil Éireann*. Having taken over the Executive Council in 1932, he helped introduce the Constitution of Ireland in 1937. With 21 years in office, he is the longest-serving Irish head of government by total days served. Biographers disagree on his legacy: Tim Pat Coogan sees his era as one of economic and cultural stagnation, while Diarmaid Ferriter argues that the austere image of de Valera was largely manufactured in the 1960s.

Archaeological site of a very large Neolithic and Chalcolithic proto-city in southern [[Anatolia]], Turkey. The settlement existed from around 7500 BC to 5600 BC, flourishing around 7000 BC, and overlooks the Konya Plain. It is notable for its large size, its apparent egalitarian social structure and its value as a well-preserved example of early Neolithic permanent settlement. The site consists of two mounds, and the eastern mound alone covers about 12.5 hectares (31 acres). James Mellaart excavated it from 1961 to 1965 and revealed 18 successive layers of buildings, although it has been strongly suggested that some of his wall paintings and figurines were fabricated. From 1993 Ian Hodder, then at the [[University of Cambridge]], led excavations that emphasized digital methodologies until 2018. The site was designated a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in July 2012.

City in central [[Poland]] and capital of Łódź Voivodeship, a former industrial center (pop., 2025: 639,890). Granted town rights in 1423 by King [[Władysław II Jagiełło]], it was annexed by Prussia in the Second Partition of 1793 and joined Congress Poland, a Russian client state, after the [[Congress of Vienna]] in 1815. Rapid growth in [[Textile|textile]] manufacturing from 1850 drew migrants, including many Jews and Germans, which made the city multinational. The Muzeum Sztuki, founded in 1931, was the first museum in Europe dedicated to collecting and showcasing modern art. During [[World War II]] the German occupiers forced the city's large Jewish minority into a walled ghetto before sending its members to German concentration and extermination camps. After a sharp decline following 1989, the city began to revitalize its downtown in the 2010s. Its National Film School is a cradle for many of Poland's most renowned actors and directors, and in 2017 the city was named a [[UNESCO]] City of Film.

French singer and lyricist, regarded as France's greatest popular singer. Born in [[Paris]], she began performing at age 14 while touring France with her acrobat father. She was discovered in 1935 by nightclub owner Louis Leplée, and in 1945 she wrote the lyrics to her signature song, "La Vie en rose." She became France's most popular entertainer in the late 1940s and toured Europe, South America and the United States, where she made eight appearances on *The Ed Sullivan Show*. Her music, often autobiographical, specialized in *chanson réaliste* and torch ballads about love, loss and sorrow. Her best-known songs include "Non, je ne regrette rien" (1960) and "Hymne à l'amour" (1949). Her last song, "L'Homme de Berlin," was recorded in April 1963 with her husband, Théo Sarapo.

French modernist painter, one of the first 19th-century artists to paint modern life and a pivotal figure in the transition from [[Realism (arts)|Realism]] to [[Impressionism]]. Born in Paris into an upper-class family with political connections, he abandoned a planned naval career and studied under Thomas Couture from 1850 to 1856. In his spare time he copied Old Masters such as [[Titian]] and [[Diego Velázquez|Velázquez]] in the [[Louvre]]. Adopting the realism of [[Gustave Courbet]], he painted beggars, singers, cafés and bullfights. His early masterworks, *The Luncheon on the Grass* and *Olympia*, premiered in 1863 and 1865 and caused great controversy with critics and the Academy, but were soon praised by progressive artists as breakthroughs toward Impressionism. They are considered watershed paintings that mark the start of [[Modern art|modern art]].

Second khan of the [[Mongol Empire]] (r. 1229–1241) and third son of [[Genghis Khan]]. He continued his father's expansion, and his successful capture of Gurganj in 1221 secured his military reputation. In 1231 he initiated the Mongol invasions of Korea, and in 1234 his armies completed the conquest of the [[Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|Jin dynasty]]. Under his nephew [[Batu Khan]] and the general [[Subutai]], Mongol forces penetrated deep into Europe, defeating Poland at Legnica and Hungary at Mohi before retreating. As an administrator he developed ortogh trading systems, methods of tax collection and regional bureaucracies, and he founded the capital Karakorum in the 1230s. Although historically overshadowed by his father, partly because of his alcoholism, he was known to be charismatic, good-natured and intelligent. He was succeeded by his son Güyük.

Autonomous and demilitarized region of [[Finland]], an archipelago at the entrance to the Gulf of Bothnia in the [[Baltic Sea]] (area 1,580 km2, or 610 sq mi). Its official language is Swedish, and its capital is Mariehamn. Autonomy was granted in 1920 and confirmed by the [[League of Nations]] in 1921. Demilitarized and politically neutral since the Paris Peace Treaty after the Åland War of the 1850s, the region's residents are exempt from universal male [[Conscription|conscription]]. Åland voters approved membership in the [[European Union]] by 73.64% in 1994.

Most populous of the eighteen regions of [[France]], centered on the capital, [[Paris]] (pop., 2023: 12,271,794). The region has eight departments, and in 2019 it generated nearly one-third of French GDP, while its per capita GDP is the highest of any French region. Its historic sites include the palaces of Versailles and Fontainebleau, and Disneyland Paris is the most-visited tourist attraction in France. Although it is the richest French region, the official poverty rate was 15.9% in 2015.

French sociologist who formally established sociology as an academic discipline and is regarded as one of the principal architects of modern social science, with [[Karl Marx]] and [[Max Weber]]. His *Le Suicide* (1897) analyzed suicide rates in Roman Catholic and Protestant populations, pioneering modern social research and distinguishing social science from psychology and political philosophy. *The Division of Labor in Society* (1893) contrasted mechanical solidarity in traditional societies with organic solidarity in modern ones. Refining the [[Positivism|positivism]] of [[Auguste Comte]], he argued that sociology should study phenomena attributed to society at large, and he became a major proponent of structural functionalism. In 1895 he set up the first European department of sociology, and in 1898 he founded the journal *L'Année sociologique*. He coined terms such as collective consciousness. *The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life* (1912) presented a theory of religion as a social institution.

French novelist, journalist and playwright, the best-known practitioner of literary naturalism and an important contributor to theatrical naturalism. Born in [[Paris]], he worked as a clerk and critic before publishing *Thérèse Raquin* (1867), his first major novel, and then began the *Rougon-Macquart* series. His childhood friend [[Paul Cézanne]] joined him in Paris. Zola did not hide his dislike of Napoleon III, and he became a major figure in France's political liberalization and in the exoneration of the army officer [[Dreyfus affair|Alfred Dreyfus]], which he pursued with the newspaper opinion headlined *J'Accuse...!* He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1901 and 1902.

Primary attendant of the [[The Buddha|Buddha]] and one of his ten principal disciples, known for having the best memory. Most texts of the early Buddhist Sutta Piṭaka are attributed to his recollection of the Buddha's teachings at the First Buddhist Council, earning him the title Treasurer of the [[Dharma|Dhamma]]. In early texts he is the Buddha's first cousin. He acted as an intermediary between the Buddha and laypeople and the monastic community, and he requested that the Buddha allow his foster mother to be ordained, helping to establish the order of nuns. At the council he was chastised by Mahākassapa for that decision. Ānanda is one of the most loved figures in [[Buddhism]], and the composer [[Richard Wagner]] and poet [[Rabindranath Tagore]] drew inspiration from stories about him.

Capital and largest city of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in northwestern [[China]]. It is the second-largest city in China's northwestern interior after [[Xi'an]], and it lies west of the Tian Shan mountains. Its population is predominantly [[Han Chinese]], although the city has one of the largest Uyghur populations in China. The name derives from Oirat words meaning "beautiful pasture." The Tang government founded the settlement as Luntai in 648 CE. The [[Qing dynasty]] took the area in 1755 during its conquest of the [[Dzungar Khanate]] and later renamed the city Dihua, a name the Chinese Communist Party reversed in 1954 by restoring Ürümqi. Since the 1990s it has developed as an economic center for western China and is home to Xinjiang University and the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory.

Leading disciple of the [[The Buddha|Buddha]], regarded as foremost in wisdom and called General of the [[Dharma]]. He was born in the ancient Indian kingdom of [[Magadha]], and with his childhood friend Maudgalyāyana he ordained as a monk under the Buddha, who named the two his chief male disciples. He was said to have become an arhat two weeks after ordination. As chief disciple he assumed a leadership role in the Sangha, looking after monks, assigning objects of meditation and clarifying points of doctrine. He was the first disciple the Buddha allowed to ordain other monks. Known for strict adherence to monastic rules, he is considered important in the development of the Abhidharma in many Buddhist schools and frequently appears in [[Mahayana]] sutras. In [[Theravada]] Buddhism he has a status close to a second Buddha. He died shortly before the Buddha, in his hometown, and his relics were enshrined at Jetavana Monastery. In Buddhist art he is usually shown to the Buddha's right.

King of the Anglo-Saxons from 924 and King of the English from 927 to 939, regarded by modern historians as the first King of England. He was the son of King Edward the Elder. In 927 he conquered York, the last remaining Viking kingdom, making him the first Anglo-Saxon ruler of the whole of England. In 934 he invaded Scotland and forced Constantine II to submit, and his victory over a Scottish and [[Vikings|Viking]] invasion at the Battle of Brunanburh in 937 gave him great prestige. He centralized government, increasing control over the production of charters and summoning leaders from distant areas to his councils. More legal texts survive from his reign than from any other tenth-century English king, and his legal reforms built on those of his grandfather, [[Alfred the Great]]. A devout king who collected relics and founded churches, he never married, and he arranged marriages for several of his sisters to continental rulers. He was succeeded by his half-brother Edmund I.

Hittite king (r. c. 1350–1322 BC) who extended Hittite authority across [[Anatolia]] and northern Syria. Before becoming king he served as military commander to his predecessor, Tudhaliya III, recovering Hittite territories. His victories over [[Mitanni]] brought a number of petty kingdoms in northern Syria under Hittite authority, and he installed his younger sons as local viceroys at [[Aleppo]] and Carchemish. The rump of the Mittanian state became a dependency of the Hittite kingdom. Relations with Egypt turned to hostility after the Zannanza Affair, in which he sent one of his sons to marry the widowed queen of Egypt and the prince was murdered. Captives he had taken caused a plague that ravaged Hittite society for at least two decades. His son Muršili II, who composed the Deeds of Šuppiluliuma, blamed the misfortune on his father's cruelty.

French mathematician and political activist whose work laid the foundations of [[Galois theory]] and [[Group theory|group theory]], two major branches of [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]]. While still in his teens, he determined a necessary and sufficient condition for a [[Polynomial|polynomial]] to be solvable by radicals, solving a problem that had been open for 350 years. A staunch Republican, he was arrested repeatedly and served one jail sentence of several months. After twice failing the entrance examination to the École Polytechnique, he submitted early papers that [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] refereed but refused to accept for publication, for reasons that remain unclear. Shortly after his release from prison he fought a [[Duel|duel]], for reasons that remain obscure, and died of his wounds. The night before, he hurriedly wrote letters outlining his mathematical insights. His complete works, just over 60 pages, were published posthumously in 1846.
